subject: radiology
title: Haemostasis and closure after arterial access

steps.tx: Manual compression still closes most arterial punctures after sheath removal in practice. The operator holds pressure over the **common femoral artery** for fifteen to twenty minutes and then keeps the leg straight. A **haematoma** forms when pressure is released too early or when the puncture sits too high. The patient rests flat for a few hours before walking, and **bed rest** protects the fresh clot. Reusing the same groin within days is avoided where the opposite side is available.
steps.say: Manual compression is still effective and closes most arterial punctures after sheath removal. The operator holds firm pressure over the femoral artery for fifteen to twenty minutes. The patient then lies flat with the leg straight while staff are watching the groin. Early release causes haematoma formation, and flat rest protects the fresh clot before walking.

steps.tx: Closure devices speed haemostasis and allow selected patients to walk sooner after procedures. **Suture mediated closure** places a stitch directly at the arterial wall and suits larger sheaths well. A **collagen plug** seals the track outside the artery and works best when infection risk is low. **Clip devices** suit calcified walls that needles cross poorly during access. Device failure always needs immediate manual compression, so compression skills remain mandatory for every operator.
steps.say: Closure devices speed haemostasis and allow selected patients to walk sooner after procedures. A suture device is useful because it places a stitch at the arterial wall directly. A collagen plug seals the track outside the artery in suitable patients. Device failure always needs immediate manual compression, so compression skills remain mandatory for operators.

steps.tx: The cutaway shows a **suture mediated closure** device passing a stitch through the arterial wall at the puncture site. The **suture foot** sits inside the lumen and anchors the needles that carry thread through the wall. The blue thread is tied outside as a **stitch knot** that pulls the wall edges together. This mechanism explains faster haemostasis after large sheaths in exam answers.

steps.tx: Blood thinning changes the timing of sheath removal after heparinised cases. **Protamine reversal** is reserved for bleeding punctures because routine reversal increases thrombosis risk. Sheath removal waits until clotting recovers, and the **activated clotting time** is checked at the bedside. Antiplatelet drugs usually continue through diagnostic work but may pause before large bore closure. **Warfarin** bridging is used only when thrombotic risk clearly outweighs groin bleeding risk.
steps.say: Blood thinning changes the timing of sheath removal after heparinised cases. Protamine reversal is reserved for bleeding punctures because routine reversal increases thrombosis risk. Sheath removal waits until clotting recovers and the bedside clotting time is checked. Bridging is used only when thrombotic risk clearly outweighs groin bleeding risk for the patient.

steps.tx: The leg gives early warning after the patient leaves the laboratory. **Distal pulse checks** compare foot pulses with the opposite side every fifteen minutes at first. A lost pulse suggests thrombosis or dissection and needs urgent review. Groin inspection looks for swelling, bruit and falling haemoglobin that suggest **retroperitoneal bleeding**. A painful pulsatile lump days later suggests a **pseudoaneurysm** and needs ultrasound assessment, while spreading bruise, numbness or pallor needs immediate return.
steps.say: The leg gives early warning after the patient leaves the laboratory safely. Staff are careful and compare foot pulses with the opposite side every fifteen minutes. A lost pulse suggests thrombosis or dissection and needs urgent review. A painful pulsatile lump days later suggests pseudoaneurysm formation, while spreading bruise or pallor needs immediate return.
